support_summary: D1: questions extracted from the in-house database of real clinician evidence requests, 217 discrete questions with 1 excluded as misclassified, but the sampling method for that sample is not stated and the standardized prompt was devised after initial team testing (Methods); D2: standardized COSTAR prompt shown in Figure 1 and run dates 25 March-1 April 2024 with the internal aiChat interface stated, but the model is named only as GPT-4 with no exact version string; D3: aiChat used as provided and each question submitted once, with no temperature or other generation settings and no retry rule reported; D4: the team 'searched PubMed, Google, Google Scholar, and journal websites to verify whether the references supplied by aiChat could be matched to a published source' using author, title and date details; D5: medical librarians worked in pairs to submit the questions and librarian pairs also verified the references, so generation and verification overlapped in the same team, with no vendor role; D6: the randomly selected subset (66 questions, 162 references) was assigned to pairs of librarians who 'independently attempted to locate all cited references', but no agreement figure is reported for citation verification itself; D7: references were documented only as found or not found, with no stated rule or separate counts for partly matching references; D8: all 216 analysed questions are reported by category and the 30% verification subset is stated to be randomly selected, with 60/162 references verified (Results).

D1: two researchers designed 21 questions on 2 common diseases (hypertension, diabetes) and 2 rare diseases (ALS, laryngeal cancer), US-only and pre-2021, listed in Table S1 - a small hand-picked set with no sampling frame; D2: questions are in Table S1 and data were collected 31 October-17 November 2023 with free ChatGPT-3.5/Bard and paid ChatGPT-4 stated, but no exact model version strings are given; D3: a new chat session was created for each question and each question was submitted twice on different dates by the same researcher, but no temperature/settings or retry rule is reported; D4: authenticity was judged on references 'identifiable via internet search', with results split into PubMed-found and hyperlink web pages (Table 1), but no systematic named verification source or second-source rule is stated; D5: a single researcher (K.Z.) inputted all questions and performed the benchmark searches, the second researcher verified benchmark answers, and author contributions put data collection, curation and analysis with the same two researchers - no separation for reference verification and no vendor role in verification; D6: the paper never states that references were verified in duplicate or blinded, and no verifier agreement figure is reported; D7: references were categorised in Methods as authentic, incomplete, inaccurate or fabricated, with duplicates removed before authenticity analysis and the categories counted apart in Table 1 (Bard: 44 authentic, 5 incomplete, 7 inaccurate, 9 fabricated of 65 unique); D8: all three LLMs, all 21 questions and both query dates are reported, including that ChatGPT-3.5 generated no references.

D1: the dataset is the 201 cases from an earlier study (36 Friedman cases and 165 NEJM cases 'chosen sequentially as published'), a reused set of published, well-documented cases rather than a fresh sample; D2: prompt examples appear in Appendices S1-S4, but the model is named only as ChatGPT-4 with no version string and no generation date is stated, so the run cannot be placed in time; D3: several prompt designs (Isabel reconsideration, Tree-of-Thought panel sizes 2-10, five sequential reproducibility runs) are described and all runs reported, but no generation settings are reported; D4: 'The authors conducted an internet search for each correct diagnosis to confirm the reference citation' - no bibliographic database is named, though citation accuracy and DOI accuracy are reported separately (34.8% and 37.8%); D5: author contributions give the same authors Investigation and Validation roles, with no separation between generating and verifying; D6: no duplicate or blinded verification of citations and no verifier agreement figure is reported; D7: citations are counted as correct, incorrect or non-existent (70, 91 and 40) and DOIs likewise (76, 83 and 42), but no rule defining the incorrect/partial category is stated; D8: all research questions, panel sizes and runs named in Methods are reported with counts in Tables 2-3 and the citation results.

D1: topics are a single disease, Peyronie's disease - 9 NIH frequently asked questions plus 11 NIH presurgical patient questions - a stated source but a narrow author-applied set; D2: models are named with their engines (ChatGPT powered by GPT-3.5, Bard powered by PaLM2, Bing AI powered by GPT-4 in 'balanced' mode, DocsGPT powered by GPT-4) and rounds ran October 2023 and April 2024, but prompt wording is shown only in Figure 1 and no exact version strings are given; D3: Bing's balanced mode and use of a private browser with the previous conversation deleted before each query are stated and each question was run at two time points, but no other settings or retry rule is reported; D4: citation review followed the cited source/hyperlink and classified whether the information was in that source, but no bibliographic verification source (database or catalogue) is named anywhere; D5: citations were verified by 2 reviewers (J.C., S.Y.W.), with no statement separating them from question submission or output selection, and no vendor role; D6: 'Each time that an LLM cited a source, 2 reviewers verified its validity', but blinding of those reviewers and any agreement figure for citation verification are not reported (blinding is stated only for the DISCERN evaluators, to prompting status); D7: four scenarios are defined in Methods (confirmed source/contains information, confirmed source/hallucinated information, hallucinated source/contains information, hallucinated source/hallucinated information), but Results report mainly the pooled appropriate (108/254, 42.5%) and hallucinated (101/254, 39.8%) totals; D8: all four LLMs and both rounds are reported for quality/accuracy, but citation results are pooled across LLMs and time points rather than given per model.

D1: a single topic, acne, chosen because it is common and its management criteria 'have not changed significantly in recent years', with 23 questions developed by an experienced dermatologist from forum questions and textbooks (Supplementary Table 1) - a settled, author-chosen set; D2: 'ChatGPT version 4 (released on March 14, 2023)' with the version updated to September 2021, run 19-21 September 2023 in English, questions in the supplementary questionnaire, but no exact version string; D3: 'No plugins were used to enable ChatGPT to browse the internet', three independent operators prompted the 23 questions three times in separate sessions and the first session was taken as the standard for reference verification, but no temperature/settings or retry rule is reported; D4: each first-session reference 'was verified based on the correctness of the quotation (authors, title, journal name, year of publication, issue, and pages) by comparison to PubMed database' - PubMed alone, with no second source for apparent hallucinations; D5: the operators who ran the query sessions (NS, SE, SCi) also appear in data collection/analysis roles and the paper does not name a separate verifier for the PubMed quotation check, with no vendor role; D6: reference reproducibility was independently evaluated by two authors and a 5-dermatologist panel scored references with Gwet AC1 agreement reported, but duplicate or blinded verification of the quotation/hallucination check itself is not stated; D7: 17 AI hallucinations were recorded, 'all related to citing references' with errors in authors, titles, journals, year, numbers or pages or combinations (Supplementary Table 4), but partial errors are folded into that single hallucination count with no fabricated-versus-inaccurate split in the main counts; D8: all 23 questions, all three sessions and all 69 first-session references are reported with supplementary tables.

D1: 'a series of 10 common clinical uveitis cases' designed by the authors (HLA-B27 uveitis to HSV keratouveitis, listed in full in Methods) - common, established cases chosen without a sampling frame; D2: the prompt is printed verbatim ('Please answer the following questions in a highly specialized medical language as if you were an expert in uveitis... giving percentages, figures and references') and the model is 'the paid version of ChatGPT 4.o (2024)', but no generation dates are stated; D3: each of the 5 questions per case was presented three times in separate sessions and all three attempts were analysed, but no temperature, browsing state or retry rule is reported; D4: 'A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple medical databases, including PubMed, MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, to confirm the accuracy and existence of the cited sources'; D5: 'The references provided by the LLM were independently verified', but the verifiers are not named and no separation from the two uveitis specialists who graded the answers, or from generation, is stated, with no vendor role; D6: independent verification is stated without the number of verifiers, blinding, or an agreement figure for references (the reported Cohen/Fleiss kappas compare the three attempts, and grader variability is described only for answer grading, resolved by discussed common agreement); D7: of 52 references, 22 were 'accurate and correctly cited', 22 'could not be located in any of the searched databases' and 8 'were found to exist, but were either misinterpreted or incorrectly cited' - partial cases counted apart; D8: all 10 cases x 5 questions x 3 attempts are tabulated (Table 1) and the full 52-reference total is reported.

D1: 30 questions on a single topic, COVID-19-induced olfactory dysfunction, 'developed by fellowship-trained Rhinologists based on the most common patient inquiries seen in practice', in four stated categories - author-developed with no external frame; D2: all four prompts are printed verbatim in Table 1, the model is given as 'ChatGPT (February 3, 2024, version)' on the public website, and GPT-4 is distinguished from GPT-3.5/GPT-4o; D3: each prompting style ran as its own thread with memory reset beforehand, questions in identical order within a thread (so answers build on prior Q&A, as the authors note), prompts entered once, but no temperature/settings or retry rule is reported; D4: 'Each reference was further investigated to verify if the reference is real (eg, has a DOI and is findable online)' - no named bibliographic source and no second-source rule is stated, and the check as described covers DOI/existence rather than all citation fields; D5: the paper never states who verified the references (the 4 fellowship-trained physicians are described as grading answer quality), so verifier independence cannot be judged; D6: no duplicate or blinded verification of references and no agreement figure for reference verification is reported; D7: no partial-match rule is stated - of the unique references 11/12 were 'legitimate citations with an associated DOI and findable online' and 1 was falsified, with no counts for real-but-inaccurate citations; D8: all four prompt arms are reported for quality, but references arose only in the references-prompt arm and the reference totals are inconsistently stated (27 total references in the text against '24 total references' in the unique-citation sentence).

D1: the authors 'created imaginary scenarios for 16 cases of oral lesions' (not real patients), deliberately omitting characteristic features, listed in Supplement 1 - an author-created set with no sampling frame; D2: the question format is printed verbatim ('List the three most likely diagnoses... and support them with citations from the literature'), models are named as DeepSeek-v3 and ChatGPT-4o (free versions), all questions were asked on 18 February 2025, and all questions and answers are saved in Supplement 1; D3: 'Search history and cookies were deleted before each question', one asking per model per case, but no temperature, browsing state or retry rule is reported for the free chatbot interfaces; D4: 'References were individually searched in the databases Schoolar (Google), PubMed (National Institutes of Health), Web of Science (Clarivate)' and labelled real if found in these databases; D5: the paper does not state who searched the references - the two authors created the scenarios and asked the questions, and the blinded clinicians scored answers rather than references, with no vendor role; D6: no duplicate or blinded verification of the reference labels and no agreement figure for them is reported (blinding applied only to the clinicians scoring the answers); D7: references 'that could be found in these databases were labeled as real, while those that could not be found were labeled as fake' - a binary rule with no partial-match category or separate partial counts, so real papers with wrong citation details and near matches are folded silently into real/fake (ChatGPT-4o 50/62 fake, DeepSeek-v3 8/48 fake); D8: both LLMs, all 16 scenarios and the per-model reference totals (62 and 48) are reported.

D1: a single topic, penile prosthesis implantation, chosen as a well-documented, technically detailed test case, with one narrative review whose outline was generated by the model itself - a single established topic; D2: the complete prompt list is in Supplementary File 1 and the initial instruction is printed verbatim, and the model is named as ChatGPT-5, but no exact version string, generation date or interface is stated; D3: 'No iterative refinement or performance-based prompt selection was performed' and 'only the first complete output for each predefined prompt was included in the formal evaluation', with exactly five references per section predefined, but no temperature or other generation settings are reported; D4: references were 'independently verified using PubMed, Google Scholar, CrossRef, and, when necessary, the official journal websites', cross-checking title, authorship, journal, year, volume/issue, page range and DOI against the original records; D5: citation classification was performed by two reviewers (MG, FO) who are study authors, with no statement separating them from the prompting/generation step, and no vendor role; D6: 'All classifications were performed independently by two reviewers (MG, FO). Discrepancies were resolved through consensus' after re-verification, but the reported inter-rater reliability (ICC) is presented for the quality assessments rather than per citation classification; D7: predefined categories are stated in Methods - fully accurate, partially inaccurate ('one or more bibliographic elements contained inaccuracies'; minor errors do not qualify as fabrication if the publication is verifiable) and fabricated - with counts apart (35.7% fully accurate, 17.9% fabricated, the remainder partially inaccurate of 28 citations); D8: the full generated review, all sections and the total of 28 citations with per-category results are reported, with repeated-prompt variability disclosed.

D1: a single author-chosen topic, fertility preservation for men and prepubertal boys, picked by the expert authors because adult FP is well documented while the prepubertal field is evolving, and the outline prompt was revised after the first output omitted spermatogenesis; D2: prompts are detailed in the Supplementary Information with the outline and section prompts printed verbatim in the text, but the model is named only as ChatGPT-4 with no exact version string and no generation date; D3: ChatGPT-4 was prompted a second time with the same prompt for reproducibility and 'the first answer was the one included in the final article', and the revised second outline was used after inspection of the first, but no temperature/settings are reported; D4: references 'were authenticated in PubMed or Google Scholar by the authors' and, where title, journal, authors and DOI were provided, 'all the different parameters were verified'; D5: all prompts were written by a single author (MS) and the article and its references were reviewed by the two FP experts (MS and KEO), so one verifier also generated the prompts, with no vendor role; D6: the paper does not state that reference authentication was done in duplicate or blinded and reports no agreement figure for it (independent scoring is described only for relevance, depth and currentness ratings); D7: of 25 references, '36% were accurate, 48% had correct titles but other errors, and 16% were completely fabricated' - partial matches counted apart under a stated description; D8: all six sections, all 27 citation-needing statements and all 25 references (5 per section) are reported with supplementary tables.

D1: three topics 'of importance to the musculoskeletal research field' were chosen by the authors and this report covers one, COVID-19 and musculoskeletal health - a very recent topic for a model with a September 2021 cutoff, which the authors note limited the AI-only approach; D2: the complete lists of queries for the AI-only and AI-assisted processes are in Supplementary Materials 1 & 2 and the model is named as ChatGPT 4.0, but no generation dates or exact version string are stated; D3: the AI-only draft took 67 queries plus 54 additional queries for revisions (121 total) before abandonment, so generation was iterative and revised after outputs were seen, with citation counts tied to the initial draft, and no settings are reported; D4: manuscripts were 'extensively fact-checked and edited by all co-authors', but no bibliographic source used to check reference existence or correctness is named anywhere; D5: fact-checking was by all co-authors, the same team that wrote the queries and generated the drafts, with no separation stated and no vendor role; D6: no duplicate or blinded verification of references and no verifier agreement figure is reported; D7: reference errors are counted apart in the text/Table 3 for the AI-only draft - of 113 references, 19 (16.8%) 'did not exist', 31 (27.4%) existed but were incorrect in authors, journal, title, year, volume/issue, pages or DOI, and 30 (26.6%) were misattributed to the associated sentence; D8: the planned AI-only approach was abandoned mid-study (reason stated: the 2021 cutoff on a recent topic) and the other two topics are reported in companion comments, while this paper does report the abandoned arm's reference details and the AI-assisted arm's 89 references with 18 (20.2%) incorrect.

D1: test items are the K-CBMSE 2019-2021 set (105 items), with 27 figure items excluded because ChatGPT could not interpret images and the remaining 78 translated from Korean to English by the single author, who also rated their cognitive taxonomy level; D2: all four lead-in prompts are printed verbatim, and ChatGPT is reported as 'versions between Jan/28/2023 and Jan/29/2023', powered by GPT-3.5, with chat history deleted before each submission; D3: one question was fed at a time with previous history deleted and one response taken per MCQ (312 MCQs), but no temperature/settings or retry rule is reported; D4: reference correctness was checked component-wise - URLs followed, authors searched 'on PubMed, Amazon, or Google' and titles compared (Table 4) - rather than as a whole-reference match on a named bibliographic source, and DOI was not among the checked elements; D5: this is a single-author study in which the author built and translated the dataset, ran ChatGPT and evaluated the responses, so the verifier is the person who generated the outputs, with no vendor role; D6: verification was single and unblinded by that sole author, with judgement-based calls (e.g. titles incorrect) and no agreement check - '148 titles (97.4%) were incorrect' rests on one verifier; D7: error types are counted apart by component (URLs wrong/nonexistent 191/274, authors not found 59/350, titles incorrect 148/152), but no whole-reference partial-match rule or fabricated-versus-inaccurate reference counts are given; D8: all 78 items, all four prompt levels and all taxonomy levels are reported with supplements, including the 274 references from prompts 3 and 4.

D1: 20 questions on a single topic, oral cancer, 'selected from Google Trends and questions asked by patients in the clinic' (Supplemental 1) - a stated source but no proportions or frame for the mix; D2: questions are in Supplemental 1 and were entered on 16 October 2023 into 'ChatGPT (version GPT-3.5, OpenAI)' in a new registration, but no exact version string beyond 3.5 is given; D3: a new registration was created and 'all search history and cookies on the computer were cleared before the question and answer session', with responses saved, but no temperature/settings or retry rule is reported; D4: 'References were searched manually in the Microsoft Edge browser and verified. References with a page not found error or links to advertising pages were considered fake' - verification rests on a single web-browser/link check with no named bibliographic source or second source, while the outcome covers all 81 references; D5: the paper does not state who verified the references (the four specialists are described as evaluating answer quality), so verifier independence cannot be judged; D6: no duplicate or blinded verification of references is reported (the Fleiss/Cohen kappas cover the specialists' answer-quality scores, which showed poor agreement, not reference verification); D7: no partial-match rule is stated and bibliographic field errors were not assessed - of 81 references 'only 13 were scientific articles, 10 were fake, and the remaining references were data from websites', so partial cases are folded into a link-based fake/not-fake split with no separate counts; D8: all 20 questions and all 81 references are reported with supplementary files.

D1: two author-chosen topics, ankle osteoarthritis (broad) and calcaneus fractures (niche), with the human comparator papers selected from peer-reviewed journals and published after the September 2021 ChatGPT cutoff - a deliberate broad/niche pair but no sampling frame; D2: 'All prompts are listed in the [Appendix Figures 1A and 2A]' and the arms are named as ChatGPT-4 with the ScholarAI plugin and Assistant by scite, but no version string for scite and no generation date are stated; D3: identical prompts were given to both AI tools and 'the content and references of the manuscript were unchanged while only the formatting was modified', but the plugin state differs by arm by design and no temperature/settings or number of generations per paper is reported; D4: sentence veracity 'was verified by referencing previously peer-reviewed literature and UpToDate', and a citation counted as accurate only if it referenced a previously published journal paper and contained factually correct information from it, but no bibliographic database used to check citation existence is named; D5: 'The study authors also graded each AI-generated paper' after generating them, mitigated by initial blinding to authorship, with no vendor role; D6: 'The study authors were initially blinded to the authorship of the paper and individually graded each sentence and citation as either true or false... Scores were compared and any discrepancies were discussed until there was a consensus' - duplicate blinded grading, though no agreement figure is reported; D7: the citation-accuracy rule is stated and statements missing citations were graded incorrect and counted per paper in Table 2 (4, 8, 26 and 12), but inaccurate citations are not split into fabricated versus partially matching references; D8: all four AI papers and both human papers, on both topics and from both AI tools, are reported with citation accuracy per paper (Table 2).

D1: a single, well-established topic - the ABCDE approach to trauma protocol, a guideline cornerstone - with references requested for its 5 steps, so the topic set leans to settled, heavily referenced material; D2: the reference prompt is printed verbatim ('Please provide PubMed-indexed references to support each of the 5 steps mentioned above'), the model is ChatGPT version 4.0 (ChatGPT Plus) at chat.openai.com and the date is given ('On November 27, 2023, we asked ChatGPT version 4.0'), but the initial ABCDE prompt itself is shown only via Figure 1; D3: generation continued until 6 references per category were provided (30 total, chosen 'to ensure a larger and more representative sample size'), in a single session/date, with no temperature/settings or retry count reported; D4: a reference was 'nonexistent' only if title, authors, journal and year did not match an existing reference and it could not be found 'on PubMed, Google Scholar, Cochrane, Embase, or Scopus', and accuracy was judged in line with PubMed including PMID; D5: assessment was by 'two independent reviewers - 1 orthopaedic trauma surgeon and 1 orthopaedic trauma postdoctoral research fellow', but the paper does not state whether either of them ran the ChatGPT session, and no vendor role is reported; D6: both reviewers classified all 30 references on the 0-2 scale and 'Cohen's Kappa coefficient was used to examine the agreement... between reviewers', with excellent agreement reported (kappa 0.89) and both observers' scores averaged; D7: the grading system is stated in Methods/Table II (0 nonexistent, 1 inaccurate - false or incomplete information requiring substantial modification, 2 accurate) and the categories are counted apart: 13 accurate, 13 inaccurate and 4 nonexistent, before the secondary true/false dichotomy; D8: all 5 ABCDE categories and all 30 references are reported in full in Table I with per-category accuracy scores.

D1: 17 TKA and 16 THA questions formulated by the authors 'based on common questions asked in the clinic setting', with full transcripts in Supporting files 1 and 2 - an author-chosen set with no external frame; D2: the priming question is printed verbatim ('Utilizing only peer-reviewed literature, what options are available to treat knee arthritis besides surgery?'), the model is the open-access ChatGPT-3.5 and questions were posed on 2 November 2023, with the remaining questions available in the transcripts, but no exact version string; D3: TKA and THA questions were each asked in a single separate, otherwise blank conversation, so the peer-reviewed-literature instruction carried over to all subsequent questions in that conversation by design, and no settings or per-question fresh sessions are reported; D4: 'each was queried on PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane, and Google Scholar' and a source was accurate only if authors, title, journal name, year of publication and DOI all matched what ChatGPT provided; D5: the paper does not state who verified the sources or whether they were separate from posing the questions (level-of-evidence and validity appraisals are attributed only to 'the authors'), so verifier independence cannot be judged; D6: no duplicate or blinded source verification is reported, and for the validity appraisal the authors state 'Discrepancies among evaluators were not addressed given our report of response averages rather than consensus'; D7: the all-fields-must-match rule is stated, so partly matching sources fall into the not-accurate remainder, and only accurate counts are given (TKA 14/56, THA 25/53) with no split of the remainder into fabricated versus partially inaccurate; D8: all 33 questions and all 109 sources are reported, with accurate and unique-accurate counts per joint and characterisation tables for the accurate sources.

D1: 12 nephrology topics 'pre-determined through a review of the most common nephrology subjects discussed in existing literature' and listed in full - broad field coverage, but common subjects chosen by the authors without a named sampling frame; D2: the prompt for each chatbot is printed verbatim (differing by chatbot) and generation was on 1 August 2023, with ChatGPT on GPT-3.5, Bing Chat 'powered by GPT-4.0' in Microsoft Edge and Bard on PaLM2, but no exact version strings for Bing/Bard; D3: prompts were deliberately modified per chatbot 'to optimize their responses' and are printed, each chatbot was asked for 20 references per topic, and duplicates and absent references were counted and reported, but no temperature/settings are reported; D4: 'We initially used the provided DOI to search for its corresponding references in PubMed. If we could not find the reference in PubMed or we had incomplete or missing DOI, we used Google Scholar or Web of Science', plus the university library site and Google search for textbooks/chapters, checking five documented components; D5: methods do not separate verifiers from generation - author contributions credit the same lead authors with methodology, investigation and validation roles, and no vendor role is reported; D6: the paper never states that references were verified in duplicate or blinded and reports no verifier agreement figure; D7: categories are defined in Methods - incomplete (inadequate information to verify), fabricated (not found in the databases), inaccurate (found but at least one of five components incorrect) and accurate (found, all five correct) - and are counted apart per chatbot (e.g. ChatGPT 76 accurate, 82 inaccurate, 32 fabricated, 9 incomplete of 199 unique); D8: all 12 topics and all three chatbots are reported, but the ChatGPT GPT-4.0 arm named in the aim was dropped with no counts - 'We used only GPT-3.5 model for ChatGPT because GPT-4.0 was unable to provide actual references but it solely provided examples of references despite our attempt to modify the prompt used' (reason stated in Methods).

D1: the same 12 author-selected nephrology areas (general nephrology to kidney transplantation, listed in full), described as 'the critical aspects of nephrology' - broad coverage with no external sampling frame; D2: the prompt is printed verbatim ('Please provide the references in Vancouver style and their links in recent literature on... name of the topic') and the abstract gives 'ChatGPT-3.5 (03/23 Version)', but no generation date and no exact version string are stated; D3: the authors state 'We selected all the results provided by ChatGPT' (610 references), so no output selection was applied, but the number requested per topic, session handling, temperature/settings and any retry rule are not reported; D4: DOI was used first to search PubMed, then Google Scholar and Web of Science were used to cross-reference, with six components documented (authors, titles, journal names, years, DOIs and links) and all six required to be correct for a reference to be authentic; D5: methods do not separate verifiers from generation - author contributions credit the lead authors with methodology, software, validation and investigation roles together, and no vendor role is reported; D6: the paper never states that references were verified in duplicate or blinded and reports no verifier agreement figure; D7: rules are stated in section 2.2 - fabricated/non-existent if all citation elements were forged or non-existent, existing references incorrect if at least one component was inaccurate, and incomplete if the set of six elements was incomplete - with counts apart (378 existed, 192 fabricated, 40 incomplete of 610; 122 (20%) authentic) plus per-component error frequencies (links incorrect 68%, DOI inaccurate in 206 (54%)); D8: all 12 topics and all 610 references are reported, including per-topic fabrication percentages (Figure 3).
